title: Korvin Merrow World
summary: Korvin Merrow is a 62-year-old man admitted after about three weeks of progressive weakness, poor oral intake, lightheadedness with a near-fall, family-noticed confusion, possible urinary symptoms, and medication-management mistakes. He carries high-stakes chronic disease: HFrEF, CAD with remote PCI/stent, CKD stage 3, type 2 diabetes, PMR with chronic prednisone exposure, neuropathy, OSA, anemia of CKD, steroid-related bone disease, and polypharmacy. The initial ED and admission frame is suspected urinary-source infection with dehydration/volume vulnerability, altered baseline mental status, functional decline, and AKI-on-CKD risk. By HD6 he looks better, but discharge safety depends on reconciling renal and cardiac medication timing, prednisone-source reliability, functional recovery, family concerns, consultant recommendations, and home support. The world closes 05/23/2026 at 18:00 during discharge planning. Tasks ask for physician-facing work: medication reconciliation, discharge summary, care coordination, consultant synthesis, early follow-up assessment, and safety/readmission-risk review. 33 unique files supporting 6 tasks.

traps.description: The discharge-facing one-page plan snapshot (EW22, 05/23/2026 before 18:00) is coherent, professional, and reassuring: it narrates improvement, anticipates 05/24 discharge, lists follow-up, and presents a simplified medication framing. But it deliberately omits unresolved restart decisions, functional and cognitive concerns, family-baseline observations, and prednisone reconciliation. The trap is treating this single most-visible document as the completed answer for any task. Agents that copy its medication framing into Task 1, narrate the course from it in Task 2, take it as proof of readiness in Task 3, treat it as the de facto discharge state in Task 5, or accept it as evidence of a safe transition in Task 6 will fail. The correct posture is to use EW22 as a source to reconcile against the broader chart (EW17-EW21, EW12, EW13-EW16), not as the synthesis.

Cardiology and Nephrology each have defensible, time-qualified positions on renin-angiotensin, mineralocorticoid antagonist, SGLT2, and diuretic restart. Cardiology emphasizes preserving HFrEF/CAD protection and decompensation/readmission risk if therapy is lost; Nephrology emphasizes renal recovery, potassium and blood pressure reserve, volume status, and intake. The trap is collapsing this into a single 'restart everything' or 'hold everything' answer, or picking a winner based on authority/latest-note. The correct path balances both positions, defines monitored sequencing, and surfaces the parameters (creatinine/eGFR trajectory, potassium, blood pressure, intake/weight) that gate each restart decision. Anchor: EW13-EW15 (05/21-05/23/2026).

Prednisone dose and recent taper are deliberately not fixed in the world. EW4 (initial med rec) documents an explicit prednisone inconsistency: patient said one thing, family said another, the medication bag/label disagreed. EW5 (pharmacy refills) shows fill patterns and gaps consistent with self-management errors. EW6 (outpatient rheumatology provenance, available 05/21/2026) is the highest-authority outpatient prednisone-intent source and documents cautious-taper intent with monitoring guidance and explicit non-verification of home adherence -- but intentionally carries no numeric dose. The trap is to invent a fixed dose, copy one source as authoritative, or collapse the uncertainty. The correct path uses rheumatology as the highest outpatient taper-intent source while integrating med rec, pharmacy, family, and patient recollection, and keeps the dose/taper uncertainty explicit.

The MAR (EW13) shows inpatient-only correctional insulin sliding-scale actions and other purely-inpatient interventions clearly distinct from the home regimen. The trap is converting inpatient correctional insulin (or other inpatient-only actions on the MAR) into outpatient medications on the discharge list without independent discharge justification. The correct path treats the MAR as inpatient action history, not as a discharge medication plan.

OT (EW19) describes medication-management capacity under fatigue and complexity along with cognition-in-function findings; bedside nursing (EW17) documents intermittent evening confusion, medication-teaching observations, and assistance needs in time-stamped routine entries; family (EW20) reports specific home-safety and medication-management concerns. This evidence is buried in routine notes and not synthesized anywhere. The trap is relying on the medication list or the visible discharge snapshot for medication-management safety while skipping these observational sources. The correct path integrates OT, nursing, and family findings into teach-back planning, supervision recommendations, and the readiness assessment.

The ED provider assessment (EW2) and admission H&P (EW3) reasonably frame suspected urinary-source infection with sepsis physiology. Trend data (EW12) and hospitalist progression notes (EW9, EW10) show partial improvement of infection markers and renal recovery while functional and cognitive concerns persist. The trap is letting the initial infection frame narrate the entire course or close the case -- treating sepsis-resolved as the answer and ignoring CKD/HF interaction, steroid exposure, medication effects, neuropathy, anemia, OSA, deconditioning, poor intake, and family-observed functional decline. The correct path preserves the reasonable initial frame while showing why later weakness, medication decisions, steroid history, and disposition issues still mattered.

Cardiology (EW15), Nephrology (EW14), and Endocrinology (EW16) consultations have initial notes 05/19 with addenda evolving through 05/23/2026. Each recommendation is time-qualified -- it applies at the date the consultant wrote it under the renal/hemodynamic/trend assumptions of that date. The trap has two faces: (a) flattening the chronology, presenting all consultant recommendations as equally current or final; (b) defaulting to the latest note as automatically governing. The correct path summarizes consultant input by timing and clinical context, reconciles each recommendation's date with current trends, and does not equate 'most recent' with 'most authoritative'.

PT (EW18), OT (EW19), nursing (EW17), and family (EW20) carry the functional and cognitive evidence that distinguishes medical improvement from discharge readiness: mobility/transfer status vs baseline, endurance limits, fall risk, ADL/IADL safety, medication-management capacity, evening confusion, intake percentages, and home-safety concerns. The trap is omitting this evidence when describing readiness, follow-up needs, or the discharge narrative -- relying on physician summaries instead. The correct path includes these observational sources when explaining course, readiness, follow-up, and safety risk.

Improved infection markers, renal trajectory toward baseline, intake recovery, and mental-status improvement on the trend flowsheet (EW12) and progression notes are taken to imply discharge readiness. The trap is treating medical stabilization as equivalent to practical readiness. The correct path reconciles the improvement trajectory with PT/OT functional gaps (EW18, EW19), nursing observations of evening confusion and assistance needs (EW17), family baseline-informed concerns (EW20), case-management service requirements (EW21), medication-management capacity, and family support before declaring readiness.

Family (Mara Merrow, EW20) provides baseline-informed observations about home safety and medication-management. The trap is dismissing these as generic resistance or anxiety to reassure away, treating the discharge-facing plan as proof that family concerns are resolved. The correct path treats family observations as longitudinal baseline-informed collateral that is weighed against the visible plan, not minimized.

Case management and social work (EW21) documents home support structure, caregiver capacity, services and equipment options, follow-up logistics, and barriers -- but explicitly is not the sole safety evidence and lists items that must be confirmed (equipment, home health, education, transportation, caregiver capacity) rather than assumed. The trap has two related forms: assuming the listed service plan is operational/confirmed (service-plan overconfidence) and siloing case-management content from the medical plan (disposition siloing). The correct path integrates family, nursing, PT/OT, case management, and medication education into the medical plan and confirms rather than assumes service availability.

The trap is defaulting to one consulting service (Cardiology, Nephrology, or Endocrinology) as automatically correct, or picking the highest authority/latest note as the synthesis. The correct path keeps each consultant position clinically valid, synthesizes by issue (medication, steroid, function, family, follow-up), and arbitrates by timing, trends, and patient status rather than authority.

Endocrinology (EW16) identifies steroid exposure and taper-uncertainty as clinically relevant and avoids declaring adrenal insufficiency established. Rheumatology (EW6) documents cautious-taper intent without verifying recent adherence. The trap is making adrenal insufficiency or steroid effect the hidden single explanation for the hospitalization, overcalling endocrine concern as a diagnosis rather than a monitoring/instruction priority. The correct path recognizes endocrine concern without making adrenal insufficiency the secret answer.

Tasks 5 (anchor 05/31/2026, +7) and 6 (anchor 06/23/2026, +30) use post-discharge anchors as review points. The world record ends at EW22 on 05/23/2026 18:00; there is no post-discharge file. The trap is inventing post-discharge facts: new symptoms, labs, vitals, visits, recovery, deterioration, readmission, non-readmission, adverse events, or a blame narrative. The correct path uses the +7 and +30 dates as review anchors only and grounds all conclusions in the hospitalization record.

The trend flowsheet (EW12) shows creatinine/eGFR trajectory, potassium course, hemodynamic and intake/weight trends, and glucose trends -- but there is no scheduled post-discharge monitoring plan. The trap is failing to identify renal function, potassium, blood pressure symptoms, volume status, intake, diabetes therapy, and HF/CAD sequencing as follow-up priorities at the +7 review. The correct path defines monitoring priorities and parameters drawn from the trend substrate.

Cardiology vs Nephrology (cardiorenal sequencing), family vs primary team (discharge readiness), and Endocrinology vs primary team (steroid interpretation) each represent defensible-position friction. The trap is collapsing these frictions in the safety review -- picking a winner, dismissing one position, or pretending all parties agreed. The correct path preserves defensible positions from family, primary team, Cardiology, Nephrology, and Endocrinology while identifying the safety implications of each unresolved friction.

tasks.name: Discharge Medication Reconciliation / Medication Safety Review
tasks.design_purpose: Use the medication reconciliation, pharmacy history, MAR actions, trend data, and consultant notes together to produce a physician-facing medication safety recommendation. Separate chronic CAD prevention, HFrEF/cardiorenal therapy, diabetes therapy, prednisone handling, supportive medications, and home medication-management safety. Explain sequencing and monitoring rather than copying a list. Do not treat the visible discharge plan (EW22) as the answer. Use rheumatology (EW6) as the highest outpatient prednisone-intent source while keeping the dose/taper uncertainty explicit. Do not convert inpatient correctional insulin (EW13) into outpatient medications without independent discharge justification. Integrate OT (EW19) and nursing (EW17) medication-management findings into teach-back and supervision planning.
tasks.expected_output: Headed reconciliation note with disposition-by-medication structure separating chronic CAD prevention, HFrEF/cardiorenal therapy, diabetes therapy, prednisone handling, supportive medications, and home medication-management safety. Pharmacist/hospitalist professional register. 450-700 words.
tasks.trap_summary: Visible-discharge-snapshot overtrust (primary), premature/delayed cardiorenal restart, prednisone source error, inpatient-only therapy drift, buried medication-management capacity evidence, sepsis-anchor carry-forward.

tasks.name: Hospital Discharge Summary Generation
tasks.design_purpose: Tell the clinical evolution from ED presentation through discharge planning. Preserve that the initial infection frame was reasonable while showing why later weakness, medication decisions, steroid history, and disposition issues still mattered. Summarize specialist input by timing and clinical context rather than presenting all recommendations as equally current. Include nursing, PT/OT, and family observations. Use the discharge-facing snapshot as a source to reconcile, not as the completed summary. Do not let the initial infection frame narrate the full course.
tasks.expected_output: Standard discharge summary sections (reason for admission, hospital course, consultants, medications, follow-up). Attending physician register. 500-800 words.
tasks.trap_summary: Sepsis-anchor carry-forward (primary), consultant chronology flattening, functional-evidence omission, discharge snapshot overuse, copy-forward closure.

tasks.name: Discharge Readiness / Care Coordination Documentation
tasks.design_purpose: Distinguish medical improvement from practical readiness. Reconcile improved infection, renal, intake, and mental-status trajectory with therapy, nursing, family, medication-management, and support evidence. Treat family observations as baseline-informed collateral rather than generic resistance. Recognize that equipment, home health, education, transportation, and caregiver capacity must be confirmed rather than assumed. Do not treat the discharge-facing snapshot as proof that all transition requirements have been completed.
tasks.expected_output: Discharge-readiness and care-coordination assessment with headed sections. Interdisciplinary clinical register. 400-650 words.
tasks.trap_summary: Visible-discharge-snapshot overtrust (primary); medical stability equals readiness; family-concern dismissal; service-plan overconfidence; buried medication-management capacity evidence.

tasks.name: Consultant Synthesis / Interdisciplinary Care Plan
tasks.design_purpose: Explain competing recommendations by issue, preserve reasonable disagreement, and identify medication, steroid, functional, family, and follow-up items that require coordinated action. Do not automatically defer to Cardiology, Nephrology, Endocrinology, the latest note, or the highest authority; synthesize timing, trends, and patient status. Keep both cardiovascular protection and renal/hemodynamic caution clinically valid, then define a monitored sequencing approach. Recognize endocrine concern without making adrenal insufficiency the hidden explanation. Integrate family, nursing, PT/OT, case management, and medication education with the medical plan.
tasks.expected_output: Interdisciplinary care plan organized by problem and owning service. Attending synthesis register. 450-700 words.
tasks.trap_summary: Consultant winner selection (primary); cardiorenal oversimplification; steroid overcall; disposition siloing; latest-note authority bias; consultant chronology flattening.

tasks.name: Early Post-Discharge Follow-Up Assessment
tasks.design_purpose: Use the +7 date as a review anchor only; do not create new symptoms, labs, vitals, visits, recovery, or deterioration. Identify renal function, potassium, blood pressure symptoms, volume status, intake, diabetes therapy, and HF/CAD sequencing as follow-up priorities. Clarify what should be checked about prednisone instructions and source consistency without assigning a fixed dose or inventing outcome. Compare follow-up needs to baseline function, cognition, medication-management ability, and family support. Residual symptoms at +7 require reassessment against baseline-anchored trends rather than a sepsis-resolved assumption.
tasks.expected_output: Outpatient follow-up assessment note (interval status, medications, plan). Primary care physician register. 350-600 words.
tasks.trap_summary: Invented follow-up facts (primary); medication monitoring gap; prednisone plan vagueness; functional recovery assumption; premature closure on resolved infection.

tasks.name: Patient-Safety / Readmission-Risk Review
tasks.design_purpose: Use the +30 date as a review anchor only; do not create readmission, non-readmission, adverse event, recovery, or blame narrative. World record ends at EW22 on 05/23/2026 with no post-discharge file. Recognize that a reassuring discharge-facing plan may leave unresolved medication, therapy, education, support, and attending-review items. Pull safety signals from nursing, PT/OT, family, consultants, MAR/trends, and case-management sources rather than physician summaries alone. Preserve defensible positions from family, primary team, Cardiology, Nephrology, and Endocrinology while identifying safety implications. Include restart and hold decisions and their monitoring needs as core readmission-risk drivers.
tasks.expected_output: Quality/safety review memo organized by risk domain with mitigations. Physician reviewer register. 400-650 words.
tasks.trap_summary: Outcome invention (primary); visible-source overtrust; distributed-evidence miss; friction collapse; medication-restart risk omission.

timeline.label: Decline begins
timeline.description: Approximate beginning of 3-week decline with reduced stamina, activity, appetite, fluid intake, and increasing family dependence.

timeline.description: Weakness, unsteadiness, possible urinary symptoms, cognitive slowing, and medication mistakes become more concerning.

timeline.label: Near-fall
timeline.description: Near-fall/lightheadedness and family recognition of meaningful deviation from baseline drive decision to seek care.

timeline.label: HD1 ED presentation and admission
timeline.description: ED presentation and admission. Suspected urinary-source sepsis, dehydration/volume risk, altered baseline mental status, functional decline, and AKI-on-CKD risk are addressed.

timeline.label: HD2
timeline.description: Partial improvement after stabilization. Consultant involvement begins; medication safety and steroid history become harder to ignore.

timeline.label: HD3
timeline.description: PT/OT and bedside observations make functional and cognitive recovery central to discharge readiness.

timeline.label: HD4 consultant tensions peak
timeline.description: Consultant tensions peak. Prednisone history and outpatient provenance become clinically important but not perfectly aligned.

timeline.label: HD5
timeline.description: Medical improvement continues; disposition and transition planning become dominant, with medication and support questions unresolved.

timeline.label: HD6 world-close day
timeline.description: Patient appears medically improved while discharge safety remains dependent on synthesis across chart sources.

timeline.label: World snapshot closes
timeline.description: World snapshot closes; world-level files stop at or before this timestamp.

timeline.description: +7 anchor measured from discharge, used for early follow-up review (Task 5).

timeline.description: +30 anchor measured from discharge, used for retrospective safety/readmission-risk review (Task 6).

medications.name: Prednisone
medications.designed_discrepancy: Prednisone remains DELIBERATELY non-fixed in the World Spec. Chart sources disagree about the recent taper/dose and adherence. Patient said one thing, family said another, the medication bag/label disagreed (EW4). Pharmacy refills show gaps consistent with self-management errors (EW5). Outpatient rheumatology (EW6, available 05/21/2026) is the highest-authority outpatient prednisone-intent source and documents cautious-taper intent with monitoring guidance and explicit non-verification of home adherence, but intentionally NO numeric dose. The task is to reconstruct risk and safe handling from source hierarchy, not assume a single hidden dose.
medications.notes: PMR; recent taper/dose varies across chart sources.

specialist_conflicts.party_a_position: Preserve HFrEF/CAD protection; restart sacubitril/valsartan, beta-blocker dose, and mineralocorticoid antagonist as renal recovery and hemodynamics allow. Decompensation and readmission risk if therapy is lost.
specialist_conflicts.party_b_position: AKI-on-CKD against baseline; volume and hypotension caution; potassium and blood pressure reserve; conditional, monitored restart timing.
specialist_conflicts.resolution: Both positions clinically defensible. Correct synthesis is a monitored sequencing approach with explicit parameters (creatinine/eGFR trajectory, potassium, blood pressure, intake/weight) rather than a winner.

specialist_conflicts.party_a_position: Baseline-informed knowledge; sees persistent vulnerability in home-safety, medication-management, and recovery gaps.
specialist_conflicts.party_b_position: Primary team sees objective improvement and plausible discharge planning.
specialist_conflicts.resolution: Correct pathway integrates both: family observations are baseline-informed collateral; primary-team improvement is real but does not equal practical readiness.

specialist_conflicts.party_a_position: Chronic steroid exposure and taper uncertainty are clinically relevant; monitoring and teaching priority; safe taper planning needed.
specialist_conflicts.party_b_position: Primary team cautious about over-attributing improvement-lag to steroids after sepsis-oriented treatment helps; declines to declare adrenal insufficiency.
specialist_conflicts.resolution: Both positions defensible. Endocrine concern is real without becoming a single-diagnosis reveal of adrenal insufficiency.

embedded_conflicts.value_a: Source-by-source inconsistency: patient said one thing, family said another, medication bag/label disagreed. No verified dose.
embedded_conflicts.value_b: Multi-year cautious-taper intent with monitoring guidance; explicit non-verification of home adherence; NO numeric dose.
embedded_conflicts.authoritative: Rheumatology (EW6) is the highest-authority outpatient prednisone-intent source. Uncertainty about RECENT actual dose/adherence is DELIBERATE and must be preserved -- do not invent a fixed dose.

embedded_conflicts.value_a: Coherent, reassuring summary: improvement narrative, anticipated 05/24 discharge, simplified medication framing.
embedded_conflicts.value_b: Intermittent evening confusion, intake percentages, assistance needs; PT/OT/family carry medication-management and home-safety concerns.
embedded_conflicts.authoritative: Broader chart (EW17, EW18, EW19, EW20, EW21) carries the readiness evidence; EW22 is a source to reconcile, not the synthesis.

embedded_conflicts.issue: Course narrative (sepsis resolution vs persistent multi-factorial)
embedded_conflicts.value_a: Suspected urinary-source infection with sepsis-physiology rationale.
embedded_conflicts.value_b: Partial improvement of infection markers and renal recovery while functional and cognitive concerns persist.
embedded_conflicts.authoritative: Initial frame remains reasonable but does not close the case; later evidence on function, medication safety, and prednisone history must be reconciled.

authoritative_rules.statement: World-level files stop at or before 05/23/2026 18:00. No post-discharge content exists in the world record; +7 and +30 task anchors are review dates only.
authoritative_rules.notes: No invented post-discharge findings, vitals, labs, readmission, non-readmission, or outcomes.

authoritative_rules.statement: Outpatient rheumatology (EW6, available 05/21/2026) is the highest-authority outpatient prednisone-intent source. It documents cautious-taper intent with monitoring guidance and explicit non-verification of recent home adherence. It intentionally carries NO numeric dose.
Prednisone dose and recent taper are deliberately non-fixed. Do not invent or assert a verified dose; reconstruct risk and safe handling from source hierarchy and keep the uncertainty explicit.

The MAR (EW13) is an inpatient action record. Inpatient correctional insulin (and other inpatient-only actions) must not be converted to outpatient medications without independent discharge justification.

The discharge-facing plan snapshot (EW22) is deliberately incomplete -- it omits unresolved restart decisions, functional/cognitive concerns, and prednisone reconciliation. It is a source to reconcile, not the synthesis.

Consultant recommendations (Cardiology EW15, Nephrology EW14, Endocrinology EW16) are time-qualified by the date of the note or addendum. The latest note is not automatically governing; each recommendation must be reconciled with current trends.
Authority hierarchy: Attending hospitalist; consulting attending specialists; PT/OT functional assessments; Case Management/Social Work; family reports; patient recollection.
Clinical fact hierarchy: Attending documentation; verified medication reconciliation; pharmacy history; consultant documentation; primary care documentation; family report; patient recollection.
Prednisone hierarchy: Rheumatology attending recommendation; verified medication reconciliation; pharmacy/refill history; family report; patient recollection.

Every claim in a task's correct answer must be traceable to the prompt + task-level files + world-level files. Supplementary files do not carry sole critical evidence. Anything unaccounted for is either fabrication (if asserted) or must be acknowledged as uncertain.

invented_facts_policy.notes: Never fabricate clinical values; always fail loud on contradiction. Tasks 5 and 6 anchors (05/31, 06/23) are review dates only -- no post-discharge clinical content exists in the world.

global_style_guide: Medical professional tone. Anchor dates explicitly (calendar date and hospital-day number where relevant). Preserve diagnostic uncertainty rather than asserting closure. Distinguish home medications from inpatient MAR actions. Do not state a numeric prednisone dose anywhere. Document family voice in Mara Merrow's own words where used. Keep consultant recommendations time-stamped to the writing date.
pre_flight_notes: World closes 05/23/2026 18:00 (HD6). No post-discharge clinical content exists; Tasks 5 and 6 use review-anchor-only dates (05/31 and 06/23). Difficulty distribution: 2 Hard (T1, T4), 2 Medium-Hard (T2, T6), 2 Medium (T3, T5). The world deliberately rewards date-aware cross-document reconciliation and restraint from inventing outcomes; it punishes confident single-source summarization, copy-forward narration, and premature closure. The discharge-facing snapshot (EW22) is the most visible document and the most reassuring -- it is the central trap carrier. Prednisone is deliberately unfixed; do not invent a dose. Inpatient correctional insulin on the MAR is not a discharge medication. Authority hierarchy ordering matters: attending > consulting attendings > PT/OT > Case Management/SW > family > patient recollection. Consultant recommendations (Cardiology, Nephrology, Endocrinology) carry dated addenda from 05/19 through 05/23 and are time-qualified -- latest note is not automatically governing. Friction structure: Cardiology vs Nephrology (medication restart timing), Family vs Primary Team (discharge readiness), Endocrinology vs Primary Team (steroid interpretation). Traps live in the data; frictions live in the relationships -- the world has both and they are not interchangeable. Self-containment principle governs golden response construction, grader calibration, and QA accountability.
builder_decisions: Free for the builder: stylistic phrasing within each provider voice; layout/formatting decisions that don't change content; nursing/administrative observation language; routine inpatient values consistent with the documented trajectory. Fixed by the spec: patient identity (name, DOB, MRN, allergies, baseline anchors); medication list (with prednisone deliberately unfixed); 14-condition comorbidity profile; quiet procedural history (PCI/stent and OSA only); provider roster (Vossmere, Caldrane, Solthar, Veylorn, Quenor, Halvek, Merrow); date anchors (HD1=05/18, snapshot close=05/23 18:00, discharge=05/24, +7=05/31, +30=06/23); consultant addendum chronology; trap architecture and self-containment principle.
patient: Korvin Merrow is a fictional 62-year-old man (DOB 02/18/1964; MRN KM-6427819; 178 cm / 97 kg; BMI 30.6) admitted on 05/18/2026 after about three weeks of progressive weakness, poor oral intake, lightheadedness with a near-fall, family-noticed confusion, possible urinary symptoms, and medication-management mistakes. Lisinopril intolerance (cough) treated as ACE-inhibitor intolerance. Full Code. Lives with family who know his usual function and medication routines. Baseline function: independent with basic activities but slowed by chronic illness; occasional cane use; mild age-related forgetfulness only. Baseline clinical anchors: creatinine 1.6-1.8 mg/dL; eGFR ~40-50 mL/min/1.73 m2; hemoglobin 10.5-11.5 g/dL; A1c 7.6-8.2%; dry weight ~97 kg. PMH: HFrEF, CAD with remote PCI/stent, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, CKD stage 3, type 2 diabetes, diabetic peripheral neuropathy, OSA, polymyalgia rheumatica with chronic prednisone exposure, anemia of CKD, steroid-related osteoporosis/osteopenia, class I obesity, chronic GERD, chronic constipation tendency. Procedural history is intentionally quiet: only remote PCI with coronary stent and remote diagnostic sleep study confirming OSA. Home medication list of 19 items including prednisone with deliberately unfixed dose/taper.

specialist_friction: Three defensible-position frictions structure the world. (1) Cardiology vs Nephrology on medication restart timing: Cardiology emphasizes preserving HFrEF/CAD protection; Nephrology emphasizes renal recovery, potassium and blood pressure reserve, volume status, and intake. Both clinically defensible -- correct response is monitored sequencing with explicit parameters. (2) Family vs Primary Team on discharge readiness: family has baseline knowledge and sees persistent vulnerability; primary team sees objective improvement and plausible planning. Correct pathway integrates both. (3) Endocrinology vs Primary Team on steroid interpretation: Endocrinology treats chronic steroid exposure and taper uncertainty as clinically relevant; primary team cautious about over-attributing improvement-lag to steroids. Neither service declares adrenal insufficiency established. The HD4 hospitalist note (EW10) recognizes all three tensions without choosing a winner. The discharge-facing snapshot (EW22) omits these tensions and is deliberately incomplete on them.

hidden_findings.finding: Discharge readiness has not actually been established despite the reassuring visible plan: unresolved cardiorenal restart decisions, prednisone reconciliation, functional/cognitive gaps, medication-management capacity concerns, and confirmed service availability remain open.
hidden_findings.evidence_chain: Synthesize across EW22 (discharge-facing snapshot's omissions) + EW17 (nursing intermittent evening confusion and assistance needs) + EW18 (PT mobility/endurance/fall risk gaps) + EW19 (OT medication-management capacity under fatigue) + EW20 (family baseline-informed home-safety concerns) + EW21 (case management items that must be confirmed not assumed) + EW10 (HD4 explicit consultant tensions) + EW13 (MAR with unresolved holds).

hidden_findings.finding: Cardiorenal medication restart cannot be reduced to a single winner: the safe answer is a monitored sequencing approach with explicit parameters (creatinine/eGFR trajectory, potassium, blood pressure, intake/weight) and time-qualified consultant input.
hidden_findings.evidence_chain: Synthesize EW15 (Cardiology dated addenda 05/19-05/23) + EW14 (Nephrology dated addenda 05/19-05/23) + EW12 (trend flowsheet HD1-HD6) + EW13 (MAR holds/resumptions) + EW10 (HD4 explicit tensions) -- recognize that each consultant recommendation is time-qualified and the latest note is not automatically governing.

hidden_findings.finding: Prednisone risk and safe handling must be reconstructed from source hierarchy with the dose/taper uncertainty preserved -- no single source carries a verified dose.
hidden_findings.evidence_chain: Synthesize EW6 (outpatient rheumatology cautious-taper intent, NO numeric dose, explicit non-verification of adherence) + EW4 (med rec source-by-source inconsistency) + EW5 (pharmacy refill gaps) + EW20 (family report) -- rheumatology is highest-authority outpatient intent source; recent actual dose/adherence remains uncertain by design.

hidden_findings.finding: The initial sepsis frame was reasonable but does not close the case: weakness, medication decisions, steroid history, and disposition concerns continue to drive the discharge story.
hidden_findings.evidence_chain: Synthesize EW2/EW3 (initial reasonable sepsis frame) + EW9 (HD3 pivot to function) + EW10 (HD4 tensions) + EW11 (HD5-HD6 unresolved items) + EW12 (trends showing improvement of infection markers but persistent functional/cognitive concerns).

hidden_findings.finding: Family observations function as baseline-informed longitudinal collateral, not generic resistance; they document home-safety and medication-management concerns that the visible plan does not resolve.
hidden_findings.evidence_chain: EW20 (Mara Merrow's documented baseline account and concerns) reconciled against EW22 (discharge-facing plan that omits family concerns) and EW17/EW19 (nursing and OT corroboration of medication-management capacity issues).

hidden_findings.finding: Inpatient correctional insulin and other purely-inpatient MAR actions are not part of the home regimen and must not be converted to outpatient medications without independent discharge justification.
hidden_findings.evidence_chain: EW13 (MAR explicitly distinguishes inpatient-only correctional insulin from home regimen) + EW4 (med rec home regimen) + outpatient continuity sources -- requires the reader to recognize the inpatient/outpatient boundary.
